html:
The Kaingang are an Indigenous people of southern Brazil, in the states of São Paulo, Paraná, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul. With about 51,000 people in 2022, they are one of the largest Indigenous peoples in the country.

They speak a Southern Jê language, close to that of the Laklanõ (Xokleng). They lived in the highland forests of araucaria pine, whose seeds were a staple food, and their society is split into two halves that marry each other.

The Kaingang fought the advance of settlers and coffee planters into their land for much of the 1800s. In 1912 agents of the new Indian Protection Service, founded by Cândido Rondon, made peace with the last resisting groups in São Paulo. Most now live on reserved lands across the south. Their neighbours included the Guarani (Mbya) and the Xetá.
